The House resumed from Friday, December 6, consideration of the motion of Mr. Hnatyshyn that Bill C-74, an Act to amend the Constitution Act, 1867 and the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act and to provide for certain matters in relation to the 1981 decennial census, be read the third time and passed; and the amendment of Mr. Prud'homme (p. 9258).

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have a chance to speak on third reading of Bill C-74 since this Bill is an important one to every Member of the House of Commons regardless of the constituency he or she represents.
This is a Bill which will affect all provinces in one way or another. In some cases it will provide a floor with respect to the number of seats. In other provinces there will be an actual increase in the number of seats. In fact, the Government brought in one amendment, and I also have an amendment on the table relating to removing the cap with respect to the number of seats for Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia. However, the second amendment is of equal importance.
In this Bill the Government adopts a policy of providing a floor for the number of seats which will be provided to provinces such as Quebec, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. Of course, the Senate floor does exist at present for other provinces in Atlantic Canada, namely, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia.
This Bill tries to restrict the growth of the House of Commons and does this by using a much higher quotient of 87,000 persons per riding whereas, under the existing amalgam program, at least in Ontario, we would have a quotient of some 80,000 or 81,000 persons per constituency. The net effect of that change for northern Ontario, I am sure, will be to reduce the representation by at least one seat in this redistribution, and as we go forward into other redistributions, it will have the same impact. That is why I proposed an amendment which would provide a floor of 11 seats under the representation which we receive for northern Ontario. It is a vast geographical area, comprising 88 per cent of the land mass of the Province of Ontario. Surely, a minimum of 11 seats out of the Ontario allocation which, under this Bill, with the amendments which have been introduced, will be increased to 99,
December 9, 1985

would be something that is not harmful to the more rapidly-growing areas of the province, yet would provide us with the kind of representation we have had for the past 10 or 12 years.
I was really disappointed when all Hon. Members of the Conservative Party, including the Hon. Member for Timmins-Chapleau (Mr. Gervais) and the Hon. Member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Kelleher), voted against the amendments, one of which was presented by myself, the other presented by the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez). We will now likely see in the next redistribution a loss of at least one seat and perhaps more. The problem with that is that we have five large cities in northern Ontario. They are very easy to serve in terms of geographical area, but it is a problem with the other six cities which represent the vast far flung regions of that area of Canada. If we try to expand those constituencies in the rural areas, we end up with an unmanageable size of constituency.
There are other problems with the Bill as well. With the existing amalgam formula we have legislation which is all but complete. Certainly, it is 90 per cent complete. All that remains is to have another debate in the House of Commons to hear objections of various Hon. Members to that redistribution. The commission would obviously want to do some fine tuning of the recommendations which will be made by various Hon. Members of the House and then we will be able to proclaim the Bill. The existing amalgam formula sets out a larger House with more Hon. Members from across the country. Certainly, this will provide additional Hon. Members for the new committee system we have, committees which at present are not well manned.
If the amendment to Bill C-74, put forward by the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), is defeated and the Bill is not sent back for further investigation and review, it would result in at least $6 million being spent for the establishment of new commissions for representation in each province across the country. The impact of that, for instance in Ontario, would be to reduce the number of Hon. Members under the existing redistribution from 105 Members to 99 Members.
Quebec will be reduced from 79 seats to 75 seats. Nova Scotia will be reduced from 12 seats to 11 seats. Manitoba will be reduced from 15 seats to 14 seats. The floor would apply in the case of Saskatchewan. Newfoundland would be reduced from eight seats to seven seats. Of course, the impact of that will be to cause a great deal of confusion because most constituencies across the country have already been through the redistribution process and they will have to go through it again if this Bill carries. We will spend another $5 million or $6 million to carry out a new redistribution.
I suppose the most difficult problem is that the impact of Bill C-74 would be not only to reduce the amount of representation in the country, but that the redistribution will come into effect sometime in the summer of 1988. No one knows when the next general election will be. However, there is a good chance it will be sometime in the spring or fall of 1988. So we face the prospect of seeing the redistribution take place during the summer of 1988, and if an alection is fought in the spring
Representation Act, 1985
of 1988, it will be on the basis of the existing boundaries, which means 282 Members of Parliament. If it is fought in the fall of 1988, it will be fought on the basis of 295 Members of Parliament. If it is fought during the summer, each political Party in the House will have to go through the exercise of establishing new constituency associations. The Government will have to go through the exercise of appointing new returning officers for any election which is carried out in the fall of 1988. We will see mass confusion during the summer of 1988 if an election is not carried out on the existing boundaries.
So we have to ask ourselves why, with the redistribution almost complete under an existing law which was agreed to by all Hon. Members, we are seeing this redistribution being brought in now. Is it the case of a desire of the Tories to gerrymander the riding boundaries? Is it an attempt to have new electoral redistribution commissions appointed by the Government? We really do not know the answers to those questions. We have many questions to ask of the Government with regard to the legislation which is now before the House.
Members on the Government side will have to ask the questions relating to the large northern ridings because they have often spoken in principle about having adequate representation from those constituencies. Yet, when the Bill was before the House with amendments last week, Members on the Government side voted against those amendments. In the next election campaign it will be very interesting to see how the Government justifies that action by its own Members.
Those are a number of the factors which must be taken into account when considering the amendment of the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis which reads:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the words "That" and substituting the following therefor:
"Bill C-74, An Act to amend the Constitution Act, 1867 and the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act and to provide for certain matters in relation to the 1981 decennial census, be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the Standing Committee on Privilege and Elections for the purpose of reconsidering Clause 2".
The Member is, of course, referring to the formula section of that Bill. The Bill also provides that debate by Members would take place in committee rather than in the House. It can be argued that the committee has a more casual atmosphere in which it is easier to argue the amendments. On the other hand, the individual Member does not have the advantage of being able to put his case to the entire House, but only to a committee of the House of Commons.
Those are some of my thoughts at third reading stage of the redistribution Bill. I am very disappointed that government Members were not willing to consider a floor for the number of ridings to be provided in northern Ontario. If we lose one seat in this redistribution and perhaps another one in the redistribution after the 1991 census, I know that municipal associations, political Parties, and many people in the North will be very disappointed and concerned that the Government

voted against the amendments which would have provided for a floor in the number of seats.
The population of northern Ontario is approximately 780,000 people. The average population per riding in New Brunswick is 69,000. New Brunswick is being guaranteed 10 seats. The principle of a floor has been adopted by the Government for a number of provinces. It seems to me that that same argument could be applied to northern Ontario which takes in most of the geography of the province. Yet the Government saw fit to turn down that argument in the vote last week.
I know that other Members want to speak on this Bill, Mr. Speaker, to argue that the Bill should be returned to committee for further debate and consideration. I hope the Government will give all possible consideration to that. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the opportunity to make a few additional comments on Bill C-74.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few questions for the Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster). He has taken the lead in the Liberal caucus in studying this legislation and has, of course, been involved in the Committee on Privileges and Elections for many years. He, therefore, knows that we did a prestudy of this legislation in committee last June, that we heard witnesses in October, and that we started a clause-byclause study of the legislation in November.
Did he not, at report stage, agree with the Government amendment which would take the cap off and allow Ontario, Alberta, and British Columbia to receive the full number of seats they were entitled to under the Government's formula? Would the Member not agree that he proposed an amendment very similar to that himself when the legislation came back to the House for report stage and that members of all three Parties agreed to that change at that time? We allowed it to pass without a recorded division.
Because of that, Mr. Speaker, I am wondering why, at third reading stage, the Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) and others started to talk about the possibility of providing more seats for the Province of Quebec. I am wondering why that presentation was not made at report stage, during committee, or at some other time by the Liberal spokesman.

Mr. Speaker, I was not here to listen to the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), but I know that he makes very good arguments in any debate.
I am sure that when he spoke on Friday afternoon he made some very, very good arguments. I am sure he was arguing that the formula which the Government has proposed to the House is simply not as fair to the Province of Quebec as was the existing amalgam formula.
When you look at the figures you can see that under the new formula Quebec will lose four more Members than it would have under the amalgam formula. It is obvious that the Hon. Member would come to the conclusion that that is not very fair to Quebec. After all, Quebec has a special position in Confederation because of the linguistic aspects. In previous
redistribution formulas Quebec has often had a base of 74 or 75 seats.
I do not find the arguments of the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis to be wrong in any way. I am sure he put them very well and argued them very effectively. If he says that the new formula adopted by the Government contains inadequacies, then 1 am sure the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) would agree. He supported my amendment for a floor in the representation of northern Ontario. I believe that all of the arguments from this Party have been completely consistent, very well reasoned, and very well argued.

Mr. Speaker, as a Member from Quebec I want to tell the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) that these proposals with respect to redistribution have had many changes. First there were the proposals which were made last year, then the Government issued a paper and subsequently a Bill. Changes to that Bill were made in committee.
Unfortunately, because there are so few Opposition Members who must be in so many committees and try to be in so many places, it is very difficult for us to keep up with every change in every Bill. That is my situation and, as a Quebecer, I am disturbed that there is no increase in seats for the Province of Quebec.
The Government says that the proposals in its Bill, compared to the proposals of the former Government, will result in important savings. Since the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) has been actively involved in this legislation, will he tell us whether there are any cost benefit studies with respect to this version of the Bill which will indicate where those savings will be? Second, does he believe that this question of redistribution should be decided on a cost benefit basis alone? Are there not political reasons which go beyond cost savings in questions such as this?

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to respond to the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) because he makes some very pertinent arguments.
In its brief presented to the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Commission, the CLC criticizes the 57 per cent growth of the Prime Minister's Office within the past year as well as the addition of electronic mailing equipment to the Prime Minister's Office at a cost of approximately $8.9 million. Arguments certainly were put before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections about those costs. Clearly there are additional costs associated with additional representation. Surely, however, the Parliament of Canada is an important institution and an increase in costs on a percentage basis would not be as great as the increase in costs that the Prime Minister's Office experienced in one year.
Furthermore, it seems to me that we should not consider these costs solely on a cost benefit basis but we should also take into account the over-all adequacy of representation in the Parliament of Canada. I believe that the committee did not
December 9, 1985

question in great detail the Government's figures with respect to cost benefit.

Mr. Speaker, I must say that I was thinking about the whole issue again on the weekend. In fact, my hon. friend from Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) gave a very clear picture of what parliamentarians are thinking. This morning, I would like to ask my hon. friend from Churchill (Mr. Murphy) again to consider what third reading means as defined in the new Standing Orders. It means that Members are supposed to have more input in the business of the House. As I said earlier, in the House our court of last resort is the third reading stage. My hon. friend will have to agree on that point. After reviewing what was done in the past, as did the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East, I reached the conclusion that we should give this matter further thought, and that is why I moved my amendment, requesting that Clause 2 be referred back to committee for reconsideration, which would also give us time to reconsider the issue of Northern Ontario.
If the Hon. Member thinks this legislation works well in Manitoba, that's fine, but I say to him that the people of Northern Ontario do not believe they have been well served by this legislation. In fact, you moved amendments that were voted down. I think this is a way to go over the entire debate on Clause 2.
At this point, I would ask my colleagues from Quebec, and I see there are some in the House, the Hon. Member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Duplessis), the Hon. Member for Mont-morency-Orleans (Mrs. Blouin), and I would like to draw their attention to this issue, and I wish they would take a minute to consider what exactly will happen. It is true that we have had some kind of agreement among the parties, that instead of going from 282 Members ... we would not go up to 310.
If we had gone up to 310, Quebec would have had four more Members. We said we did not want the House to increase from 310 to 343 to 369 by the year 2001. That was too much, it was too expensive and it didn't make any sense. The individual Member's voice would be lost in the general clamour. So we were going to try and find a formula that while dealing fairly with the demands being made by the West and Ontario because of their larger population, would also help us reduce the number of Members. That was the origin of the initial proposal to have six Members more, then in the course of the debate we got as far as seven Members, and then on second reading, after hearing all witnesses, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn) came in with another proposal, when he said it would not be six or seven but thirteen. So the people said: Why not! Fair enough, 13 will do. But now we are thinking it over, after all that is the purpose of the third reading, I am asking myself why we are here on third reading, Mr. Speaker. To think it over, that is why.

Upon reflection, we came to the conclusion that, if Quebec were to have four more seats under the previous Liberal formula, four more seats out of 28, it is now rather strange that we should not even get one out of 13. We had all agreed to an averaging formula under which Ontario would have two more Members, Alberta three more, and British Columbia two more. We thought it was fair and reasonable because of the increased population.
But we have to remind ourselves that, according to the Liberal formula boosting representation to 310 Members, British Columbia would have had five more seats. Now it will get four more. According to the previous Liberal formula, Alberta was to have six more seats, now it will gain five new ridings. I can understand that those people-your colleagues, my friends from Quebec-would not disagree today since they get practically as many new seats under the new formula as they did under the other one. But Ontario should feel shortchanged since it was supposed to get ten new Members under the old formula and now it ends up with only four. And again I remind you that the old formula gave four new seats to Quebec, while the new formula of the President of the Privy Council works out to zero.
So it is a matter of equity. That is why I think the committee should reconsider this provision, and we will see what they decide whenever we do get back to third reading.

Mr. Speaker, I draw to the attention of the House the poor performance of the Government in administering the Native Economic Development Program. This Program was an initiative of the previous Government. The Program was established to support and promote the economic development of native people. Applicants are becoming increasingly frustrated with the inability of the Minister responsible, the Minister of State for Small Business (Mr. Bissonnette), to deliver. Months go by without any decisions.
One such casualty of this snail's pace decision making is the Yukon Indian Development Corporation. Its application has been in the system for 14 months. It was approved by the program's native advisory board over a year ago. Still, it awaits the Minister's decision.
In addition, Sir, there are over 50 proposals that have been submitted under the community based element of the program. Only two have been approved. Now we learn that this entire element in the program is being frozen.
I call upon the Minister and the Government to make up their minds. Do they want this program to continue? It could be the vehicle for moving forward native-operated businesses in the country, if the political will is there.

EAST TIMOR-CONDITIONS FOLLOWING INVASION BY INDONESIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must confess to a deep sense of shame that I have sat in this House of Commons for over five years and never once have I raised the subject of East Timor. Neither has any other Member of my Party, of the Liberal Party or the Conservative Party.
Ten years ago, with no advance preparation, Portugal withdrew from East Timor, a colony it had occupied for over 400 years. Indonesia moved into this vacuum and invaded. Since that time one-third of East Timor's 650,000 people have either been killed or starved to death.
East Timor has the highest infant mortality rate in the world. Of every 1,000 babies born, 211 die before their first birthday.
In 1978, Glen Shortliffe, Canada's Ambassador to Indonesia was given a conducted tour of East Timor. He was shocked by the desperate need for food, clothing, and basic medical care. His report to the Canadian Government has never been released.
In spite of this genocidal oppression, the East Timorese have continued guerrilla warfare against the Indonesian occupation. Canadian officials have regarded the Indonesian takeover as a fait accompli. They do not think this slaughter on an isolated island is important enough to disrupt our growing trade relations with Indonesia where Canada is now the third largest investor and where last year we hosted-

REPLIES TO QUESTIONNAIRE DISTRIBUTED IN CALGARY EAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently I distributed some 57,500 copies of a questionnaire throughout my constituency of Calgary East dealing with matters of concern to most Canadians. Approximately 5,400, or some 9.5 per cent, were completed and returned. Since this is a very gratifying and representative return, 1 now wish to share the results with all our Members.
The questions, with the results, are as follows: Do you think free trade should exist between Canada and the United States? Answer: 73 per cent, yes; 13 per cent, no. Are you in favour of Canada participating in the Strategic Defence Initiative, SDI that would shield North America from any external missile threat? Answer: 73 per cent, yes; 17 per cent, no. Should the federal Government sell part of its shares in Petro-Canada to the Public? Answer: 73 per cent, yes; 17 per cent, no. Should shares in Petro-Canada be given free of charge to Canadians? Answer: 29 per cent, yes; 61 per cent, no. Are you in favour of Charles Ng and Joseph Kindler being extradited back to the United States? Answer: 93 per cent, yes; 4 per cent, no. Are you in favour of capital punishment being fully restored in Canada? Answer: 83 per cent, yes; 10 per cent, no. Are you in favour of abortion on demand? Answer: 47 per cent, yes; 41 per cent, no.
I hope the Government takes note of these figures and acts accordingly.

subtopic: SUPPORT FOR DENIAL TO FEDERAL PENITENTIARY INMATES
SUPPORT FOR DENIAL TO FEDERAL PENITENTIARY INMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a recent federal court case involving the rights of prisoners to vote in the Quebec election has reopened the issue of granting
December 9, 1985

prisoners the right to vote. I believe, for the sake of law-abiding citizens everywhere, that we should not allow convicted prisoners in federal penitentiaries the right to vote in federal elections.
Our society is built on the rule of law and adherence to a set of fundamental principles of justice and order. Therefore I find it incomprehensible that an individual, who has violated the rights of others and has clearly disregarded the responsibilities of citizenship, should be given a right so fundamental to the duties of good citizenship.
Surely we put people in jail to punish them. Surely that punishment involves denial of the very rights and privileges these people choose to abuse by committing a crime. I believe it offends every Canadians's sense of justice and morality to consider even allowing a convicted murderer like Clifford Olsen the right to vote.
We must take a stand now to uphold the values and principles of law-abiding Canadians and say no to the granting of voting privileges to convicted criminals.

subtopic: CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL TOBACCO MARKETING AGENCY
CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL TOBACCO MARKETING AGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's tobacco farmers have waited long enough for the Government to make a decision to proceed with the establishment of a national marketing agency which will help producers get a fair price from the multinational corporations which deal in tobacco.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) says that he does not want to lose his job by setting up an agency. In response, I would remind him that in the 1984 election campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised to establish a board. More recently he advised a tobacco farmer from Port Burwell that the Government would act quickly to establish a national tobacco marketing agency.
The Government must start making decisions and must start soon, or the continuing uncertainty will not only affect our tobacco farmers but all other farmers and businessmen who are waiting to make important business decisions.
The bottom line is that the Government promised to establish an agency for tobacco farmers. Where is the action? In June, 1984, the Conservative Party, when in opposition, prevented the Liberal Government from passing legislation which would have allowed this issue to be resolved long ago. The Tories caused the delay then and they are causing the delay now. Without immediate action we could see 600 tobacco farmers going out of business in the very near future.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to the attention of all Canadians the contract held by Greenwich Canadian Testing of Western Ontario, from Government of Canada file reference No. 27ST; March 1985, and the research and development publication entitled Canadian Probes in Space: New Instruments Developed for Space Research. This contract for $6,600 is for the following:
Research relating to the development of methods of testing and analysis of pencils.
No doubt the method of testing pencils is something the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has long cherished learning more about. Our national pencils should no doubt be of the highest quality, easy to sharpen, capable of going up and down on paper, as well as leaving clear lines when going in circles. The eraser, of course, should be well attached to ensure that no time is lost in correcting Government errors. For a Government so set on red ink and red circling, one would hope that some of the 66,000 pencils to be tested will be red.
To be serious for a moment, for a Government which is prepared to slash pensions and family allowance, for a Government set on selling out our country to the lowest bidder, as in the case of de Havilland to Boeing, for a Government which will allow tainted tuna and buffalo onto our kitchen tables, let us hope that the Prime Minister is having these Government pencils tested to get the lead out and do something good for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday, during the questioning on buffalo meat, and again this morning, the Chamber and the people of Canada witnessed an attack on the meat inspection system of Canada. The attack was fuelled by a desire for political gain, but was based upon ignorance of the disease tuberculosis and of the meat inspection system.
The meat inspection service of Canada has handled thousands of similar cases in cattle herds in its history. Meat inspectors, many of them veterinarians, have applied their judgment to decide when meat from animals exposed to any disease is fit to eat. When tests are ordered, they are conducted primarily for disease control reasons, not for meat inspection purposes. Through this scheme, the meat inspection system has played a large role in nearly eradicating tuberculosis in cattle and, as a result, in much of the human population.
I agree with Dr. Brian Wurtz, President of the Canadian Veterinary Medical Association, who has publicly aired his support of the meat inspection service. Why should a different

December 9, 1985
system be proposed in this case? Our system is successful. It is renowned around the world. It is a crime against every Canadian to smear a good service and to spread false rumours about such a fine system, for purely political reasons.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian mining industry produces some $45-billion worth of mineral products each year. This represents about 11 per cent of Canada's Gross National Product, and the sale of these products accounts for some 30 per cent of Canada's exports. Despite this, the mineral industry has experienced more difficult problems in the last four years than at any time in the last 50 years.
The Government has been doing much to help the industry through this difficult period. Federal-provincial mineral agreements have been signed with nine provinces, including recent agreements with Quebec, Ontario, and British Columbia. The capital gains tax exemption and the fuel tax rebate have been very beneficial. Most beneficial, however, have been the mining flow-through share arrangements for exploration expenses which have stimulated exploration all across Canada, and in particular in the Province of Quebec.
In the past year the federal Government provided over $1.3 million to Canadian universities for crucial research in the earth sciences. Work by the Geological Survey of Canada has identified the biggest offshore coal field in eastern Canada, and stimulated a major gold exploration program in northern Saskatchewan. Unique solutions were found to assist production at Faro in the Yukon, and the construction of a new lead smelter at Trail, British Columbia. These and other measures have considerably improved conditions for the Canadian mineral industry during one of the most difficult periods in its history.

subtopic: EFFECT OF CHANGES ON SECURING BENEFITS

speechtext:
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, I want to protest changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act which will come into effect on January 1, 1986. These changes will cheat Canadian workers of benefits for which they have paid and were expecting. On that date, early retirement pensions will be counted toward reducing the granting of unemployment insurance benefits even when the individuals involved are ready and willing to work.
I would like to protest these measures not just because of the unjust principle on which they are based but also because this action was taken unilaterally by a Government which said it was going to consult. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) has stated repeatedly that consultation took place before these measures were introduced. These changes were certainly not endorsed by the participants in the Government's economic summit which took place last March. In fact the only clear agreement which came out of that summit was a petition signed by two-thirds of the participants calling on the Government to revoke these changes. No studies were conducted to determine the impact of these changes on older workers and on the different regions of the country.
The Government has turned a deaf ear to the many protests which were made against these policies. On January 1, older workers will be dealt a serious blow unless the Government listens to reason. I am asking the Government to withdraw this foolish policy before it is too late.

Mr. Speaker, despite often publicized difficulties facing Saskatchewan agriculture, I would like to draw to the attention of the House the general state of the economy in my home Province of Saskatchewan. The economy in the province has been improving since the election of this Government. Employment continues to climb. A total of 17,000 new jobs were created since the election of the Government. Bankruptcies were down 10 per cent in the first 10 months of this year. Business investment intentions are up 9.6 per cent over last year's levels. Housing starts in October alone were up a whopping 237 per cent.
In the energy sector, in the first 10 months well completions totalled 3,085 compared to 2,420 over the same period last year. This represents an increase of almost 28 per cent since the election of the Government.
There is also the energy Accord and what it has done for western Canada. Oil trade has been freed up to provide strong encouragement for investment. The Western Accord recognizes Saskatchewan's desire for a policy relying less on Government handouts and intervention and more on the opportunities of a free market-place. It is measures like these that have led to a growing, vibrant, improving Saskatchewan economy.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is clear from our projections that de Havilland would have been in a loss position for 1986, depending on the source of the estimate, of between $50 million and $75 million, and it would have required an additional $125 million of cash injection. Oral Questions

The Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) gave me the required notice of his intention to request an emergency debate under Standing Order 31. The purpose of that order, as I think all Hon. Members know, is to provide a means of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration. One of the conditions laid down in the Standing Order is that the matter proposed for discussion must relate to a genuine emergency calling for immediate and urgent consideration. The matter proposed by the Hon. Member as a subject for emergency debate is certainly an important one. However, I do not think that it conforms to the concept of a genuine emergency as envisaged by the Standing Order.
Furthermore, this important matter was debated very recently and was taken to a vote. It was the subject chosen for an allotted day on Tuesday, December 3, and the House, through its vote, has already expressed a view on the matter. The Hon. Member is, in fact, asking for another debate on the same issue in the form of an emergency debate. In the circumstances, I cannot find that the application meets the requirements of the Standing Order.

Mr. Speaker, what we have just heard must be one of the most shameful actions taken by the Government to date.
Oh, oh!

Let me say why it is so shameful. Redistribution is a matter of great concern to every Member of Parliament. It is not a matter that is central to any policy or platform outlined by the Government of Canada and time allocation ought only to be imposed with respect to matters that are absolutely essential and central to the policy of the Government. Those matters are very rare because as far as I know, the Government does not have a manifesto or policy to lead the country. It is wandering around in darkness, grasping at straws here and there, trying to pretend that it represents
December 9, 1985

leadership. This matter is not central to the Government but one which is of concern to every constituency in this country and to every Member of Parliament.
We know that in theory the readjustment of political boundaries is a purely technical exercise. It could be considered even more so in this day of high technology when all of the necessary information can simply be fed into a computer. However, Members know that this approach is unacceptable. Although no one wants to see constituency redistribution dealt with in a partisan fashion, we know that the redistribution of boundaries is a highly political issue and a concern to every Member of Parliament. It is of concern to every constituency in this country and an issue that is fraught with many hazards.
I never believed for a moment that the right of Members of Parliament to express their grievances and raise their concerns would be cut off-quillotined-in this objectionable and unworthy fashion. The Government says that it believes in Parliament. Before the Conservatives became Government, I recall when they often talked about their belief in an open Parliament and that Parliament should have the opportunity to express its views. Yet closure is being imposed and debate is being limited on a matter of great concern to individual MPs. The opportunity for Members of Parliament to express their concerns on behalf of their constituents is stifled.
Let me return to the theme about avoiding partisanship in the redistribution of boundaries while at the same time emphasizing that it is a political issue. I use the word "political" in the best sense of the word, being of concern to all citizens. The House will be aware that in 1964 it was the Hon. J. W. Pickersgill who brought in the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act that we are amending today. When the House resumes consideration of this Bill, I want to begin at that point and tell the House where we have moved from that moment and how we have come to this very dark time in the history of the Parliament of Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a very great honour for me to co-sponsor this resolution proclaiming Raoul Wallenberg as an honorary Canadian citizen. It is a great significance that it is sponsored by members of the three Canadian political Parties, and that hopefully it is enjoying the consent of the House of Commons today and will enjoy the consent of the honourable the Senate tomorrow on International Human Rights Day, 1985. I am proud, as a member of the Liberal caucus, to be associated with my colleagues, the Hon. Member for Laval (Mr. Ricard) of the Conservative Party and the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) of the New Democratic Party, in sponsoring this resolution. In so doing, we not only enshrine Raoul Wallenberg's name into our Canadian history, but his name will enshrine ours. To paraphrase Abraham Lincoln, the world will little note nor long remember what we say here, but it will always remember what Raoul Wallenberg did to salvage the dignity of the human spirit. Still today, much of the world lingers in the darkness of oppression. However, human rights will ultimately prevail and the dawn will surely come. Brightly will it shine upon the tombs of heroes. Thus will shine the dawn.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CITIZENSHIP ADVISABILITY OF PROCLAIMING RAOUL WALLENBERG AN HONORARY CITIZEN OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to join with other Hon. Members of the House of Commons on this occasion. There are occasions recorded by historians when individuals, without regard for personal safety, put everything on the line for their fellow man. The opportu-

December 9, 1985
Raoul Wallenberg
nity for adequate recognition of actions such as these are few, and the sacrifice that goes with such actions is frequently lost in the books which record it. Today, we in the House of Commons have an opportunity to correct or at least to recognize both of those situations.
Raoul Wallenberg, it goes without saying, showed remarkable courage and bravery on behalf of Jews who lived in Hungary during the Second World War. That this is well recorded and documented, no one denies. Today we can recognize his incredible commitment to humanity.
Raoul Wallenberg could have lived in Sweden in a life of relative comfort throughout the Second World War. He need not have faced what he ultimately faced.
This act we propose today is unique and I contend that it is, however, a fitting act. 1 urge my fellow Members of Parliament to extend to Raoul Wallenberg the highest honour available to us-our desire to share our citizenship.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my comments, I asked a few questions when the Hon. Member for Laval (Mr. Ricard) moved that his Bill be withdrawn.

It was to withdraw Bill C-234. I will read what was on the Order Paper because 1 think it is very important in terms of what I would like to say today:
Second reading and reference to the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration of Bill C-234, an Act to proclaim Raoul Wallenberg to be an honorary citizen of Canada.
I said that if I had a chance to speak, I would give my consent, and I did. The new rules provide that every Member can give consent or not, unless we change the rules.
Then my colleague from Toronto, the Hon. Member for Eglinton-Lawrence (Mr. de Corneille), asked for similar leave from the House in terms of his own Bill. The Order Paper reads:
Second reading and reference to the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration of Bill C-233, an Act to proclaim Raoul Wallenberg to be an honorary citizen of Canada, and requesting his return to freedom.
There again I gave my consent. Because I wanted to speak on the Bill, I had prepared myself to do so. Those Bills were to be referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration. However, I gave my consent, because you are damned if you do and you are damned if you don't. Because I believed so strongly in the day which we will celebrate tomorrow, I thought it would be in bad taste for me not to give my consent. We knew what the debate was to be all about.
The Hon. Member for Laval read his own motion, as did the Chair, so I will not read it. It is similar to the motion presented by my colleague from Toronto. Therefore I will not read his motion.
I have no doubt as to the qualifications of Raoul Wallenberg. Tomorrow, many Canadians just like many colleagues of
ours from the three political Parties, will begin to know who Raoul Wallenberg is. People ask who Raoul Wallenberg is. They would like to know more about him so I will say more.
The reason I wanted to send the two Bills standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Laval (Mr. Ricard) and the Hon. Member for Eglinton-Lawrence (Mr. de Corneille) to committee is that for many years, I wanted to find a way to honour people who deserve it, either because they had rendered some service to Canada or because they had worked beyond the call of duty in the cause of human rights. I was going to propose today that we send the Bill to the Committee on Multiculturalism, a new committee, to have it look into how one could be made an honorary Canadian citizen and to consider Mr. Raoul Wallenberg as one of the first recipients of the honour.
Since we were not told this by those who proposed the motions, I will do so. Canadians would like to know that this is a very exceptional gesture on the part of Parliament. This will be the first time ever an honorary Canadian citizenship will be given to someone in the world. We were not told that.
I would like it to be on record that all of what is taking place tonight is supposed to have been debated in each of the three caucuses and debated in the Senate. It was debated in caucus as we were told by the Hon. Member who spoke just before I did. He also said that he already has the assurance that the Senate will give its consent. That means there must have been much agreement before today, much of which I am totally unaware. I would like to be on record saying that I was totally unaware of much of that agreement.
In the few moments left to me, I would like to reflect on what will happen tomorrow, December 10, 1985. I recall that tomorrow is to be Human Rights Day. I recall that many people have spoken on this issue before. It is not a new issue and Canadians should be told that. 1 would like to put on record some of the history behind the Raoul Wallenberg motion so that people do not feel that they have been taken by surprise.
On October 7, 1980, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Eglinton-Lawrence, spoke on behalf of freeing Mr. Wallenberg from the Soviet Union. I would like to render homage to a very fine old colleague of ours, Dr. Stanley Hudecki, the former Hon. Member for Hamilton West, who on November 18, 1980, also raised that issue. I would like to put that on record for those who tomorrow will begin to ask who is Raoul Wallenberg.
On December 10, 1980, the Hon. Member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) raised a question as to the fate of Mr. Raoul Wallenberg. On December 18, 1980, the same question was raised by David Smith, a colleague of ours who was defeated, the former Hon. Member for Don Valley East, on Order of the House No. 43.
Canadians will want to know who this person is who will be the first person ever to be made an honorary Canadian citizen. I would have preferred to have had a much larger debate on
December 9, 1985

this issue and a much larger audience because we are about to give what I consider to be one of the best citizenships in the world to this person.
On August 4, 1982, my esteemed colleague, the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger), also raised the question of Raoul Wallenberg. Since then, no one has asked to give him Canadian citizenship. Now I come to the words of a very important, fine gentleman, our own Mr. Speaker. I would like to render him homage and read part of what the Hon. Member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley) said on May 17, 1984, as recorded on page 3822 of Hansard, in the first mention of offering Raoul Wallenberg Canadian citizenship:
Mr. Speaker, the League for Human Rights of the B'nai Brith, supported by the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews, the Swedish-Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Chinese-Canadian National Council, and the Federation Internationale des Droits de l'homme, have asked the Secretary of State (Mr. Joyal) to declare Raoul Wallenberg an honorary citizen of Canada, and I wish to add my voice in support.
He went on to speak quite well and quite extensively on the matter.
Today my colleague went second. I would like to render him homage because on April 15, my colleague went first by introducing Bill C-233, an Act to proclaim Raoul Wallenberg an honorary citizen of Canada and requesting his return to freedom. This motion was immediately followed by that of an esteemed colleague of ours, the Hon. Member for Laval, who on April 18, 1985, suggested the same thing. That was the first time we started talking about honouring a foreigner as an honorary Canadian citizen.
I make no secret of the fact that 1 would have preferred to send the entire matter immediately to a committee of the House with instructions for the committee to inform us of how in the future we should proceed in honouring honorary Canadian citizens and to recommend as one of the first, if the committee so wished, Mr. Raoul Wallenberg. Some people, in their wisdom, decided to proceed otherwise. That is why there was a slight confusion earlier in the debate when we had to ask consent of the House to withdraw a bill, consent of the House to withdraw another Bill, consent of the House to introduce something that could only be introduced at the end of December and consent of the House for something that would have to be introduced again at the end of December. I went along with that, but I would like to be on record, for the benefit of colleagues of mine who may still have some doubt, that I believe very strongly that one of the greatest sicknesses that must be fought continuously is anti-Semitism in the world. If Raoul Wallenberg was able to do what he did, it is because there were people called Nazis who in their fury wanted to dispose of a certain group of people known as those of the Jewish faith. I believe this must be denounced and for that reason, Raoul Wallenberg could qualify as one of the first honorary Canadian citizens.
Having said that, I would like to repeat that I want to know something of which only the House Leader and my two colleagues could inform me. Is this the way we will proceed in the future? When I am not a Member of the House of Commons, others will need to know how to proceed when they
Raoul Wallenberg
want to honour someone as an honorary citizen of Canada. The way to proceed would be to present Bills or motions and to ask for the generous consent of all Members of the House for the great qualification which some people may have in order to proclaim them honorary citizens.
I repeat that I do not oppose the motion which is before the House. 1 think it would be impossible for me to oppose it, although in reading it I find it difficult to understand why one would want to honour someone by including certain of the divisions which may have taken place. Some people say Raoul Wallenberg is still alive, which is mentioned in the Bill. I also do not think it is necessary to talk about the Soviet Union in a Bill which proposes to honour someone in Canada. To say what he has done would have been sufficient and positive. The anti-Soviet sentiment in the Bill is not my style. I believe we must keep the door open in respect to talks between the two big powers.
If it is true that Raoul Wallenberg is still alive, that he is in prison and that the Soviets know his whereabouts, then there are many ways in which to honour him other than the way which is proposed. However, I am not the master of this place. Each Member has his own way in which to proceed. This is not my way.
I would like to conclude by saying again that tonight I have been asked by Members: Is it the first time we will have a Canadian citizen-

I would like to tell the House that what we are now doing is to honour someone whose actions will be described tomorrow in the newspapers and to honour him not only as an honorary Canadian, but as the first ever honorary citizen of Canada. [English]
There are only two honorary citizens of the United States. The Americans have used this great gesture only twice. The first time was to proclaim Sir Winston Churchill an honorary citizen. Of course, to me, that concept is universal in the western world. The second time it was utilized was to honour Raoul Wallenberg.
I hope my two colleagues who have proposed this Bill are aware of the hearings which took place before a subcommittee on human rights, part of an international organization connected with the committee on foreign affairs of the House of Representatives in the United States. A person who was saved in Hungary by Raoul Wallenberg when he was 15 years of age later became a congressman in the United States Congress. He is a Congressman for the State of California. He was very diligent in his representations with respect to Raoul Wallenberg. President Reagan signed a Bill with respect to proclaiming Raoul Wallenberg an honorary citizen.
I was asked several months ago how we in Canada can honour Mother Theresa in a very concrete way for the great work she does. She is alive. We sometimes prefer to honour those who are dead. However, we do not know whether or not

December 9, 1985
Raoul Wallenberg
Raoul Wallenberg is dead or alive. I know members of his family are still alive. I know he helped a great many people who are now Canadians. I know some of them. Some of them are Hungarian of Jewish religion who now live in Canada, some in Montreal.
I think Raoul Wallenberg is properly suggested for such an honour. Perhaps the nest time the occasion arises we could look around the world and choose someone in order to show that Canada is a country which stands not only for human rights but that it is a country which does a great deal for its neighbours, as Mother Theresa is doing. To me that is very important.
On the eve of that great day, December 10, I would like Canadians to reflect on what human rights really means. There are too many people in the world who are too selective with respect to coming to someone's defence. Whose human rights are we ready to defend? There are many people who organize groups for the defence of human rights of this and that. On the eve of that great day I think Canadians should reflect not only with respect to the human rights of a group, because there are many, but on the human rights of individuals. Many people have come forward to say that in the Middle East there are issues with respect to human rights which should be raised in the House of Commons. I wish to echo those sentiments here today. I hope that my colleagues in the House will learn that when we talk about human rights we should not be selective. We should talk of human rights in general. When we consider honouring someone we should do so in particular, as the House has done today in honouring Raoul Wallenberg.
I now know the road to follow, and for the information of those Canadians listening and who will read this debate, in order to honour a second or third person as an honorary Canadians, one must go through the House of Commons. One must find a champion in the House of Commons who will put forward a motion. I intend to propose one with respect to Mother Theresa. Then one must ask the permission of one's colleague to withdraw his Bill and then ask the three Parties for unanimous consent. If the case is a bona fide one we can then proclaim the person an honorary citizen. Then, around the world, we can say that in Canada we not only honour our own citizens but people from outside of Canada.

subtopic: RAILWAYS-CARRIAGE OF DANGEROUS GOODS THROUGH TORONTO
RAILWAYS-CARRIAGE OF DANGEROUS GOODS THROUGH TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish tonight to take Members back for a few moments to the great Mississauga train derailment of a few years ago. I know that you can recall the time, Mr. Speaker, just as vividly as I can and just as vividly as can the people of Missussauga, the people from Metropolitan Toronto and the people from the areas surrounding Metropolitan Toronto. This was a great jolt to the people of Mississauga, Metropolitan Toronto and the surrounding areas.
Before the Mississauga train derailment, there had been on a number of occasions in the past in Canada and in the United States-and, for that matter, in other parts of the world- other catastrophes of this sort where there were chemical spills, explositions, fires and great devastation as a result of train derailments. I suppose we in the Metropolitan Toronto area felt that this kind of thing could never happen to us. Perhaps we were asleep at the switch and were not paying too much attention. But, certainly, the Mississauga train derailment jolted our attention. It caused all of us to reappraise the situation and think for the first time about what could really happen in these cases.
You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that at the time of the Mississauga derailment we were faced with, first, an exposition, then a fire, then the escaping of chlorine gas which caused the evacuation of a great many people. In fact, 225,000 people in Mississauga were evacuated for a period of some six days. That, of course, changed the way in which the people of Metropolitan Toronto and the surrounding area thought about this whole problem. Many citizens immediately became concerned and, as a result, organized a variety of citizen groups to try to deal with the situation and spearhead some changes in the law. Second, they inspired local Government to become concerned enough to try to bring about some changes. Third, the provincial Government was inspired to get involved as well. Finally, of course, pressure was put on the federal Government of the day to investigate the situation to see what could be done.
Out of all that came the Grange Royal Commission of Inquiry which looked into the Mississauga disaster. During its investigation it found a great many individual problems with the transportation of dangerous goods and commodities through the Metropolitan area. One of the major problems it found was that dangerous goods were in effect being shunted back and forth through the heart of Metropolitan Toronto, not for any specific purpose, but just because it was convenient for the train to take the goods through Metro Toronto, bring them back and then, perhaps, take them back and forth three or four times befor they were marshalled on to their ultimate destination, which may have been western Canada.
Out of the Grange Report came a number of recommendations, many of which have already been dealt with. But there is still a major problem because there are still many carloads of
Adjournment Debate
dangerous commodities being shunted back and forth through the heart of densely-populated Metropolitan Toronto every day of the year. That is of particular concern to my constituents because the train derailment in Mississauga was only about 30 minutes away from the heart of my constituency. My constituency has the main lines of two of the major railways the CPR and the CNR, running right through the Don Valley which cuts through the middle of my constituency and I suspect there are dangerous goods being transported on those rail lines right at this very moment. Obviously, that is of concern.
The backyards of some of my constituents abut the railway right-of-way and if anything happens they would certainly be in the front line of a disaster. But it is not just the people whose backyards abut this area who have a problem, it is everyone within one or two miles of the area. As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, we can have something called a "bleavy" when there is a derailment of a train carrying dangerous goods which causes an explosion that perhaps can cover one or two miles, devastating and wiping out the population in that area.
What can be done about that? There are a number of things which can be done and right now the Toronto Board of Education is doing one of those things, that is, carrying out evacuation drills. It is teaching the children how to evacuate the schools in the event of a spill of chemical materials near a railway track.
There are other things which can be done as well. The speed at which the trains are moving could be slowed down. There could be a rerouting of those trains and in fact a relocating of the rail lines themselves. Recently, there have been a couple of inquiries by the Railroad Transport Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission which is looking into the situation. There was one in Metropolitan Toronto where it was decided that nothing would be done, and another in Vancouver and Victoria where it was decided that as of the 1st of January the transportation of dangerous goods through the high-density areas of Vancouver and Victoria would be banned.
It is time we addressed this problem in Metropolitan Toronto. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that on December 4, 1 asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) what he was doing about the situation. He indicated in reply that he intended to set up a task force to deal with the problem. That task force, we hope, will be forthcoming before the end of the year. I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary tonight will be able to tell us when we are going to have that task force, what the terms of reference will be, whether it is going to deal with the question of rerouting or relocation and whether it will deal with the question of speed.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, this is the Christmas season. It is the season of hope, and I trust that the Parliamentary Secretary will give us hope tonight for a safer 1986. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that one of the citizen groups which has been dealing with this matter in Metropolitan Toronto, MTRAC, or the Metropolitan Toronto Residents Action Committee, is looking for some answers, as are all of the people in

December 9, 1985

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
subtopic: RAILWAYS-CARRIAGE OF DANGEROUS GOODS THROUGH TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate my hon. colleague's remarks. I would like to take notice of his comments. Six p.m. came rather sooner than we had expected this evening and, unfortunately, the Parliamentary Secretary could not be here at this time. However, we will definitely take notice of the remarks and give an answer back to my colleague.
In view of the fact that our colleagues opposite who had given notice that they wanted to ask a question on the Adjournment Debate are not here, although the Parliamentary Secretary is here to answer one of the questions, I suggest that we will co-operate with the Table in rescheduling tonight's Adjournment Debate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: RAILWAYS-CARRIAGE OF DANGEROUS GOODS THROUGH TORONTO
speechtext:
I thank the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary.
The motion to adjourn the House is now deemed to have been adopted. Accordingly, the House stands adjourned until tomorrow at 11 a.m., pursuant to Standing Order 3(1).
The House adjourned at 5.48 p.m.
Tuesday, December 10, 1985
